title: Alaska Landslide Sent a Tsunami 1,580 Feet Up a Mountain
summary:
In August 2025, a mountainside in Alaska suddenly collapsed into a long, narrow inlet of the sea called a fjord. The falling rock created the second-highest tsunami in recorded history. Now scientists have described what happened and the warning signs that came before it.

The landslide happened in Tracy Arm, near the South Sawyer Glacier. Water and debris rushed 1,580 feet (481 meters) up the other side of the fjord. That is higher than the top floor of Taipei 101, a famous skyscraper in Taiwan. The force of the water scraped the fjord's walls down to bare rock. Luckily, it happened just after 5 a.m., and no ships were nearby. A tour ship had visited the glacier only about 12 hours earlier.

Researchers at the Alaska Earthquake Center studied the event. They noticed a pattern: several big landslides in recent years have happened right where glaciers are shrinking. When the ice melts away, mountains seem to become less stable.

Before this landslide, there were clear clues. The glacier below had shrunk back more than a third of a mile in two months. Heavy rain had soaked into cracks in the mountain, which can push rock closer to breaking. And in the days before the collapse, instruments recorded thousands of tiny earthquakes, called tremors, coming from the slope.

The scientists believe these signs could have triggered alerts for nearby ships and buildings at least a day early, if a monitoring program had existed. They suggest a yellow-orange-red alert system, like those used for avalanches and volcanoes.

No landslide warning system of this size exists in the U.S. yet. The researchers say building one would take teamwork between state and federal agencies.
why_it_matters: As glaciers shrink, more mountains near the sea may become unstable, so learning to read warning signs could help protect ships, visitors and coastal towns.

background_read: A landslide happens when rock and soil on a steep slope suddenly break loose and slide downhill.
Glaciers can act like a support at the base of a mountain, so when the ice melts and shrinks back, the slope above can become less stable.
When a huge amount of rock crashes into water, it pushes the water away in powerful waves, which is how a landslide can cause a tsunami.
Instruments called seismometers record ground shaking, and scientists study those signals to spot unusual activity before and during disasters.
